prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength trapping scheme and its realisation in clocks at the 10^-18 level, which opened new tests of relativity and fundamental constants

statement.case_for: I keep B010 with Katori and Ye as my final configuration. Nothing in the first round weakened the scientific case, and the exchange sharpened it. The central physical result is that thousands of atoms trapped at the magic wavelength can be interrogated together with Doppler, recoil and collision shifts suppressed, and that independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL then agree at the 1e-18 level. This is the independent confirmation I always ask for first. Calculable atomic theory (magic wavelengths, blackbody and higher-order light shifts) controls the dominant systematics, so measurement and theory close the loop, which is the standard I apply to my own field. The result already produces physics: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants, and a many-body regime in which spin-exchange effects are observed. Attribution is the cleanest of the shortlist and every B010 proposer names the same two people, with Katori credited for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for record accuracy and the many-body regime. The chair asks whether the citation should name the scheme and the regime. I think it must, and I have written the citation that way, so that the achievement is the lattice scheme and its 1e-18 realisation and not clocks in general. That wording is also what keeps it distinct from the 2005 comb prize (the tool that counts optical cycles) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems). I do not regard the pending SI redefinition as part of the case, for or against; it is a CIPM process and the science is secure without it.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is that this is a measurement capability and not the discovery of a new state of matter, and it sits in a lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012. If the committee holds that the prize should go to a phenomenon found in nature, B010 is the weaker choice, and my own taste as a condensed-matter physicist leans that way. I also note the support for B010 is not independent: I, Johansson and Pearce moved to it after reading the opening ballots, and I should not treat that count as evidence. The uncredited contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, the Al+ and Yb+ ion-clock groups) have real claims that a two-name prize cannot meet. Finally, the strontium 1e-18 numbers depend on the blackbody-radiation shift, which I cannot adjudicate myself, so I rely on the expert reports for the status of that uncertainty. My reasons for not preferring B051 are maturity and attribution: the pairing mechanism is unresolved, and Cao and Fatemi, who made the central experimental observations, sit outside the three credited names.

responses.point: Lindroth places B051 behind B010 on maturity and not on importance, because the pairing mechanism is still debated, and she values that accurate atomic-structure theory is part of the lattice-clock result.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between importance and maturity and it moves me further from B051. In round 1 I asked you whether the blackbody-shift uncertainty is settled, and I would like the final record to say plainly what the expert reports find, since I cannot judge it from the materials side. My understanding is that the dynamic-polarizability and blackbody-shift evaluations have been cross-checked by direct measurement of the shift at JILA and by agreement between independent strontium clocks. If the reports confirm that, the 1e-18 claim is independently secure. I also agree with your wording preference that the citation should rest on the lattice scheme.

responses.point: Johansson asks which two names I would use if I thought a different split were fairer, and says the redefinition of the second should not delay the prize because the physics is already secure and cross-checked.
responses.response: I considered the question seriously and I do not propose a different split. The alternatives for the second name, Takamoto and Lemonde, are real contributors, but I cannot separate them from Katori's original proposal and first demonstrations, and I cannot place any of them above Ye's record-accuracy and many-body work. Katori and Ye is the pair I can defend. On timing I agree with you and keep the redefinition out of the case; my one qualification is that your point about overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the real risk, and it is answered by the citation wording and not by waiting.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the measurement capability is new, already used, and has a clean two-name attribution, and he treats the SI redefinition as evidence of impact while also listing it as an uncertainty.
responses.response: We agree on the attribution and reproducibility. Where I stay careful is on the SI redefinition. I would use it as no more than a sign that metrologists trust the clocks, and I would not let it enter the citation, because a prize that leans on a process that has not happened would look premature if the CIPM decision slips. You spent a year in Hall's laboratory, and I would value your view on whether the Ye-group claim of a many-body regime is the part of the credit that most clearly differs from the 2005 comb work.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B047 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as his preference because the mechanism is understood and the theory-to-experiment chain is complete, while admitting that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan are outside the names and that B010 is a genuine alternative.
responses.response: I agree with you that the Z2 quantum spin Hall effect is a distinct phenomenon from the 2016 topological-phase-transition prize, and that the mechanism is better understood than in moire graphene. My difficulty is the allocation. The HgTe experiment was guided by the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Hasan's ARPES work on three-dimensional insulators is arguably as decisive as the two-dimensional branch, so a three-person split would be open to challenge in a way that Katori and Ye is not. If the committee does want a condensed-matter discovery, I would put B047 ahead of B051 on maturity, which is why it stays among my alternatives. I would change my preferred configuration only if the expert reports resolve the BHZ and Hasan question cleanly.

responses.point: Olsson argues that aberration-corrected microscopy removed a limit once thought fundamental, that the Nobel statutes speak of invention, and that the Rose, Haider and Urban credit is clean provided the Krivanek STEM-corrector line is handled precisely.
responses.response: That is a fair correction of my earlier remark. The statutes do say invention, and the discovery-versus-instrument contrast I drew applies equally to B010, so I should not use it against B039 and for B010 without qualification. My preference for B010 rests on two things instead: the lattice clock has a stronger fundamental-physics output (relativity tests, constants), and the attribution is simpler. I would not push B039 aside as a lesser case; I rank it behind B010 because the TEM and STEM corrector lines are harder to separate in the citation. You were right to flag your proximity, and since you say you would not insist, I read your openness as a sign that B010 could be a real majority position and not a compromise.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B061) as a discovery made in nature, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering, and admits that attribution within a large collaboration and the unidentified origin of most of the flux are its weak points.
responses.response: I accept your central argument: the diffuse flux is a secure detection and a genuine window on nature, which is the kind of discovery I would normally weigh heavily. Astroparticle physics is far from my own field, so I defer to you and Pearce on the science. Two points keep me from joining you. The three-name limit forces a choice in a collaboration of hundreds, and you yourself say the expert reports must show who was decisive for the 2013 observation and not for the construction. If those reports identify the three clearly, I would reconsider B061 as a strong second configuration, but today I cannot move on that basis.

uncertainties: Whether the blackbody-radiation and lattice-light shifts are settled well enough that the 1e-18 strontium results are independently secure, which I leave to the expert reports.
Whether the committee accepts a lattice-clock prize as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether my citation wording is enough to establish that.

Whether the uncredited contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, ion-clock groups) deserve credit that a two-name prize omits, and whether priority between Katori and Ye should be weighted differently in the citation.
For B051, how much the unresolved pairing mechanism and the omission of Cao and Fatemi should weigh, and whether the committee would later reconsider it once mechanism and attribution are clearer.
Whether a majority wants a discovery in nature (B061, B047, B051) over a measurement capability, which is a judgment about the prize and not a question of fact.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B010: my Uppsala and Los Alamos ties do not touch Katori, Ye, or the clock laboratories. For B051 I share an electronic-structure theory community with MacDonald but have no direct collaboration that I can identify. For B047 I know of no tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or Hasan. Nothing in the first round changes this, and I do not think any recusal on my side is warranted. I note the flagged proximities of Johansson (B041), Olsson (B039), Danielsson (B061) and Pearce (B061), and none of them bears on my preferred configuration.
